princeton:20000.summary: Only one arm of this bronze processional cross survives. It ends in a medallion engraved with the bust of a saint, identified by the museum as St Theodore, and beside it a mourning figure raises a hand; Greek words engraved along the arm read 'Behold your mother', Christ's words from the cross. The crucified Christ himself, at the lost centre, is now missing except perhaps for a trace at the broken edge.
facts: Princeton records the fragment as Byzantine, possibly from Constantinople, 10th century; it measures 14.5 × 9.6 cm.
It belonged to the sculptor Elie Nadelman and passed through the dealer Joseph Brummer before Frank Jewett Mather Jr. bought it for the museum in 1933.
princeton:20000.notes: The Crucifixion is named in the museum title but only the end of one arm survives; Christ is not clearly visible. The reading of the inscription is mine from the photograph.

walters:W.539.163R.summary: In this page from a Gospel book illuminated by T'oros Roslin, the greatest master of medieval Armenian painting, Christ stands radiant in a blue mandorla on Mount Tabor, flanked by Moses and Elijah while Peter, James and John fall to the ground in awe. Roslin combined Armenian, Byzantine and even Western influences with a refined, elegant line and jewel-like color. The manuscript was made at the patriarchal see of Hromkla, a crossroads of cultures in the age of the Crusades.
facts: T'oros Roslin worked at the patriarchal scriptorium of Hromkla under Catholicos Constantine I; seven manuscripts bearing his signature survive, dated between 1256 and 1268.
Roslin expanded the cycle of Gospel illustrations far beyond earlier Armenian practice, placing small narrative scenes throughout the text.

Kept for centuries in churches at Sebastia (Sivas), the manuscript remained there until the deportation of the Armenians in 1915; Henry Walters acquired it in Paris in 1929, and his widow gave it to the museum in 1935.
A statue of Roslin stands outside the Matenadaran manuscript library in Yerevan, Armenia.

Q805442.summary: Rising above the fields outside the small town of Świebodzin in western Poland, this crowned Christ with outstretched arms was for some years the tallest statue of Jesus in the world. It stands on a raised mound, wearing a golden crown as Christ the King. The monument was the vision of a local parish priest, Fr. Sylwester Zawadzki, and was built mainly with donations from parishioners, Poles abroad and local businesses.
facts: The figure itself is 33 metres tall, one metre for each traditional year of Christ's earthly life, topped by a gilded crown 2–3 metres high (sources differ), on a mound about 16.5 metres high.
It was completed on 6 November 2010 and consecrated on 21 November 2010, the Solemnity of Christ the King, by Bishop Stefan Regmunt.
In 2018 it was reported that internet antennas had been mounted in the crown, sparking a public debate before they were removed.
